France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
The disruption continued early on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address.
Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray, appearing before France's National Assembly, said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
NuÃ±ez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said, and confirmed the use of stun grenades was being suspended "until the facts surrounding this case have been clarified".
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste BÃ©hal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired.
According to the local prefect, the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The stun grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon, but sends out small rubber pellets when it detonates.
"When there is suspicion of disproportionate force, there are always judicial investigations," NuÃ±ez said, affirming that the government was "here to protect high school students".
The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the decision to halt the use of stun grenades, saying it had been based "on emotion".
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.

French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.
The prime minister has accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of trying to "sow chaos" ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April. He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details.

NuÃ±ez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."
